newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Shell Nigeria plans model flowstation project.
newsitem.headline: Shell Nigeria plans model flowstation project.

text.p: By the first quarter of 1998, Royal Dutch Shell's Nigerian unit will have completed the upgrading of its Jones Creek flowstation, planned as a model for others located in the Western Division, a senior official of the company said.

"The Jones Creek flowstation is being upgraded with up-to- date technology and latest standards which will be a model facility concept," Chris Haynes, technical manager of The Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria, told visiting reporters on a tour of the station.
"We have planned to progressively graft this model facility concept into all other flowstations located in this area."
He did not say if this would be extended to other flowstations located in the Eastern Division.
The Jones Creek flowstation, which was commissioned in 1970, is located in the swamps near the midwestern Warri town.
It is Shell's biggest flowstation in Nigeria and was originally designed to produce 150,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil, Haynes said.
He said another aspect of the project, approved and begun in October 1994 and now in its third phase, was developing mutually-beneficial relations with the host communities.
"For example, we have been able to provide amenities that will facilitate productive fishing for the fishermen in the Okerenkoku community neighbouring Jones Creek flowstation," he said.

Isaac Aposhi, head of the flowstation said: "The entire project will enhance maximum efficiency and reliability during crude production, ensure that less gas is flared during production, less oil spillages and generally reduce waste and emissions."
But ocassional operational problems and a shortened lifespan of oil wells supplying the flowstation have limited its production capacity to about 109,000 bpd.
Shell has 35 flowstations in the Western Division currenlty producing about 450,000 bpd.
Haynes did not provide the cost for upgrading of the flowstation, which would include the provision of electronic instrumentation and metre systems, new pumps and improving its drain systems.
Shell said on Thursday it had launched a gas gathering project, the first in a series of plans aimed at eliminating flaring by 2008.
Its swamp and land flowlines replacement programme was also in progress and nearing completion, it said.
The company has been under constant attacks from residents of oil-producing areas and environmental campaigners for alleged ecological devastation.

It faced local and international pressure to shut down its operations in Nigeria following the hanging last November of nine minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa for murder, despite worldwide appeals for clemency.
Shell pumps about 950,000 bpd of oil, which is half of Nigeria's two million daily production.
